flags.short_description: Ping scan: which hosts are up (no port scan)
flags.long_description: Sends ICMP echo, TCP SYN to 443, TCP ACK to 80, and ICMP timestamp by default. Doesn't probe any ports — fastest way to map live hosts on a subnet.

examples.explanation: List every responsive host on your local /24.

flags.short_description: Treat all hosts as up (skip discovery)
flags.long_description: Useful when targets block ICMP or you already know they're online. Otherwise nmap may skip hosts it thinks are down.
Sends a SYN, never completes the handshake. Faster and quieter than -sT, and the default when nmap runs as root. Requires raw-socket privileges.

examples.explanation: Default fast TCP scan against a single host (run as root).

warnings.text: Most IDS still log SYN scans. Use --scan-delay or -T2 for stealth.

flags.long_description: Asks the OS to fully open a TCP connection to each port. Slower and noisier than -sS, but works as an unprivileged user. The default when nmap is not run as root.

examples.explanation: Standard TCP scan that works without sudo.

flags.long_description: Probes UDP ports. Slow, because closed UDP ports are silent and nmap must wait for ICMP unreachable replies. Pair with -sV for service identification.

warnings.text: UDP scans are slow — expect minutes per host.

flags.short_description: Probe open ports to identify service / version
flags.long_description: After finding open ports, nmap sends service-specific probes (HTTP banners, SSH versions, etc.) to identify what's running. Adds time but transforms results from 'port 22 open' to 'OpenSSH 9.6'.
Compares responses to crafted probes against nmap's OS database to guess the remote operating system. Needs at least one open and one closed port to work well.

warnings.text: Confidence varies — read the 'OS guess' percentage in the result.

flags.short_description: Aggressive: enables OS detection, version, scripts, traceroute
flags.long_description: Shorthand for -O -sV -sC --traceroute. The 'just give me everything' button. Loud — easy to detect.

warnings.text: Equivalent to running default scripts; some are intrusive. Don't use against systems you don't own.

flags.long_description: Single ports, ranges, or comma-separated lists. Prefix with T: for TCP and U: for UDP when scanning both. Examples: 22, 1-1024, T:80,U:53.

examples.explanation: All TCP ports — slow but exhaustive.

flags.long_description: Equivalent to --top-ports 100. A reasonable default when you want a quick look without scanning all 65,535 ports.

flags.short_description: Scan the N most common ports
flags.long_description: Uses nmap's nmap-services frequency data. --top-ports 1000 is the default behavior of nmap with no port flag.

examples.explanation: Quick first look at the 20 ports most likely to be open.

flags.long_description: Pre-baked timing presets. -T3 is the default. -T4 is a good speedup on reliable networks. -T5 trades reliability for speed and may miss results.

examples.explanation: Fast scan suitable for a LAN.

warnings.text: -T4 / -T5 against external networks can trip rate-limits or be flagged as abuse.

flags.long_description: Show progress info and intermediate findings as the scan runs. Stack -vv for even more.

flags.short_description: Only show ports that are open
flags.long_description: Hides closed and filtered ports from the report — much easier to read on busy targets.
Equivalent to --script default. Pulls in a curated set of safe-ish scripts that surface useful info on common services (HTTP titles, SSH host keys, SMB shares, etc.).

warnings.text: 'Default' is broadly safe but not guaranteed non-intrusive. Skim the categories you're enabling.
